This study examines the computational expenses of calculating Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) energies and forces alongside Density Functional Theory (DFT) energies and forces. We demonstrate that the cost of QMC energies and forces scales with the effective pseudopotential valence charge ($N_v$) as $N_v^2$ and $N_v^3$, respectively. In contrast, the cost of DFT energies and forces scales as $N_{el}^4$ and $N_{el}^5$, where $N_{el}$ represents the number of electrons. Consequently, the ratio of QMC to DFT computational costs for energy-related calculations follows $N_v^2/N_{el}^4$, which simplifies to $1/N_{el}^3$ for neutral systems. This relationship indicates that the expense of performing QMC energy calculations diminishes rapidly as system size increases. Furthermore, we find that the ratio of QMC forces to DFT forces follows $1/N_{el}^2$, suggesting a similar rapid decline in force calculation costs as system size grows. These findings underscore the potential for QMC to deliver highly accurate forces for large systems at a computational cost comparable to that of DFT.

This study examines the dissemination of claims regarding widespread voter fraud during the 2020 U.S. presidential election through a dataset of 1.5 million tweets. Our analysis reveals that these claims were predominantly shared by users with low follower counts, while the most prolific sharers were accounts dedicated to political commentary. Furthermore, Twitter's own moderation efforts were found to be effective, as the platform removed or limited the visibility of the vast majority of tweets containing such claims.

We establish that the Hausdorff dimension of points exhibiting maximal emergence equals $\dim_{\mu}(\mathcal{M}_0)$, where $\mathcal{M}_0$ represents the set of points with maximal dimension. This result applies to SRB measures and extends to broader contexts, including those involving non-uniformly hyperbolic systems.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely recognized for their ability to learn efficient representations of data. This study investigates leveraging VAEs to enhance the efficiency of deep Bayesian neural networks (DBNNs). We introduce a novel architecture that integrates a VAE with a DBNN, enabling the network to operate with a significantly reduced number of parameters. The proposed method is evaluated on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, demonstrating that it achieves competitive performance relative to full-precision models. Furthermore, we assess the approach's resilience to adversarial attacks, confirming that the VAE-enhanced DBNN maintains robustness against such threats.

This study introduces a novel methodology for calculating electron transfer reaction rates, integrating the strengths of instanton theory and Marcus theory. By utilizing a Marcus-inspired framework, we derive a closed-form expression for the path integral partition sum that accounts for both nuclear and electronic degrees of freedom. This approach offers a robust description of activated reactions, including tunneling effects, and provides a clear, interpretable depiction of reaction mechanisms. We validate the method's accuracy through its application to a prototypical two-level system, demonstrating excellent agreement with rigorous numerical solutions.

This study introduces a novel approach for trajectory tracking that addresses the challenge of unmodeled dynamics, specifically focusing on unaccounted-for time delays. By integrating a predictor into the control loop, the proposed method effectively mitigates these delays, thereby enhancing tracking accuracy. The work further establishes sufficient conditions for input-to-state stability (ISS) regarding the closed-loop system and derives explicit formulas for the ISS gain. These analytical findings are validated through simulations involving a robotic arm.

This study examines the electronic, thermal, and thermoelectric characteristics of the alloy $\text{La}_{0.7}\text{Sr}_{0.3}\text{MnO}_3$ doped with tungsten, utilizing first-principles calculations. The results indicate that the introduction of a tungsten-derived impurity band within the energy gap significantly enhances electrical conductivity. Furthermore, the tungsten impurity states located in the valence band contribute to an increase in thermopower. Consequently, the thermoelectric figure of merit is markedly improved by these tungsten states, suggesting that tungsten-doped $\text{La}_{0.7}\text{Sr}_{0.3}\text{MnO}_3$ holds promise as a viable thermoelectric material.

This work introduces a probabilistic framework for the perfect sum problem, which involves determining the likelihood that the sum of $n$ independent random variables equals a specific target value. We demonstrate that this method yields more accurate results than existing techniques by leveraging advanced numerical algorithms. Furthermore, the approach is applied to the analysis of the distribution of the longest run in $n$ coin tosses.

This article introduces a straightforward algorithm for identifying a specific element within the rational function field $\mathbb{F}_q(x)$ whose $m$-th power yields a rational function possessing a numerator and denominator of degree $m$. This outcome demonstrates that the polynomial $x^m-a$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{F}_q(x)$. The study concludes by applying the algorithm to investigate the irreducibility of the polynomial $x^n-a_0-a_1x^m-a_2x^m$, where $m$ divides $n$.

Recent years have seen significant strides in model checking technologies, which have directly fueled the development of strategy synthesis algorithms for parallel software. This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of these algorithms, which are derived from model checking theory, and further details their practical implementation.

We introduce a novel, optimized metasurface imaging architecture that converts a wide field of view into a single focal plane. This system utilizes a single metasurface to generate a specific set of spatially localized, non-Gaussian, and mutually incoherent point-spread functions (PSFs) for every field point. By leveraging the mutual incoherence of these PSFs, the imaging process can be effectively reconstructed via compressive sensing. This methodology enables the system to achieve a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) even under noisy conditions, while simultaneously offering a high degree of flexibility in design.

We present a theoretical investigation into the dynamics of a hydrogen atom subjected to a linearly polarized, chirped laser pulse. By employing the classical approximation, we analyze the atom's response to varying field strengths and pulse durations. Our findings indicate that this simplified classical model effectively captures the dynamical behavior of hydrogen under intense laser fields. Furthermore, we identify that specific combinations of field strength and pulse duration can drive the system into high Rydberg states, with the maximum achievable state contingent upon the pulse parameters.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has garnered significant attention recently, with numerous methods leveraging unlabeled data to enhance model performance. However, the majority of these approaches rely on the assumption that the training dataset is a single, homogeneous distribution, a condition that is often violated in real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel SSL framework that capitalizes on the presence of multiple data distributions within the unlabeled set. Our approach begins by synthesizing augmented samples from distinct images to create a new pseudo-dataset. We then employ a self-supervised learning strategy to derive a feature extractor capable of capturing the diverse distributions within this pseudo-dataset. Subsequently, we utilize a multi-branch architecture to train a classifier that learns from both the original training images and the generated pseudo-samples. Empirical results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art SSL techniques across various datasets.

This study introduces a novel methodology for designing experiments to investigate stochastic gene expression, leveraging mathematical optimization to select the most suitable experimental configurations. We propose a framework that utilizes the discrepancy between the performance of a model and actual experimental data as the metric for information gain. This approach is applied to a model of gene expression, where the goal is to identify parameter values that align with observed data. We demonstrate that the method can be adapted to address various optimization challenges, including selecting the best experimental design, estimating parameters, and performing model selection. Furthermore, we illustrate the approach using a simple model of transcriptional regulation, showing how it can simultaneously estimate parameters and address gene expression noise.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a potent class of machine learning algorithms, finding extensive application in domains such as chemistry, materials science, and drug discovery. However, the optimal configuration of graph hyperparameters—such as the number of layers, the aggregation method, and the readout mechanism—remains a critical challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically learning these graph hyperparameters by formulating the task as a variational inference problem. By employing a variational encoder, the method learns a distribution over hyperparameters conditioned on the input data, thereby enabling the inference of an optimal posterior distribution. This framework is designed to be flexible and compatible with various existing GNN architectures. Empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms both manual tuning and other automatic search strategies.

Quantum algorithms like the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) are anticipated to outperform classical counterparts on optimization tasks, yet their practical efficacy is hindered by noise. This study examines the impact of coherent dephasing errors on QAOA training dynamics. We demonstrate that such errors can cause the emergence of barren plateaus, rendering gradient-based optimization ineffective. Furthermore, we quantify the extent of this phenomenon as a function of the number of layers (p) and the count of qubits (n). Our findings indicate that the region where barren plateaus dominate expands as p increases, but contracts with higher n. Consequently, the adverse effects of coherent dephasing are more pronounced in deeper circuits and smaller problem instances.

Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) has garnered significant attention within the computer vision field due to its practical applications and inherent difficulties. Although numerous methods have been proposed, most rely on a standard pipeline that first extracts features and subsequently matches them using distance metrics. This paper introduces a novel approach that bypasses explicit distance computation by employing a differentiable sorting mechanism to align query and gallery features. This strategy eliminates the need for a separate feature matching module, thereby reducing computational overhead. Furthermore, we propose a novel loss function designed to enhance the discriminative power of these features. Experimental results on two prominent public datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a methodology for generating high-fidelity synthetic time series data for power systems by merging the strengths of both data-driven and physics-based techniques. The approach utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to synthesize high-resolution time series that accurately reflect the statistical characteristics of specific nodes within a power network. To ensure physical consistency, the method incorporates a set of custom loss functions that enforce adherence to power system laws. The resulting data are validated to be both physically accurate and statistically representative, with the specific loss functions serving as the primary mechanism for ensuring physical validity.

This study examines the convergence of perturbed iterative methods for solving variational inequality problems defined on a closed, convex subset of a real Hilbert space. The analysis incorporates perturbed iterative processes featuring non-linear operators and external perturbations, establishing sufficient conditions for convergence to a unique solution. The theoretical findings are validated through illustrative numerical experiments.
The text presents a verification of the Fuchsian group axes conjecture for all symmetric and cyclic groups, encompassing both the real and quaternionic cases.

This study examines the potential decay of $\rho$ quarks into a $t$-channel top quark and a $Z$ boson, a process predicted by certain extensions of the Standard Model. Utilizing 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV from the LHC's ATLAS detector, the analysis targets the $\rho \to tZ$ decay by reconstructing the $tZ$ system via its decay products into a $t\bar{b}$ pair and a $t\bar{b}$ pair. The study finds no evidence for a signal, thereby establishing upper limits on the branching fraction of the $\rho$ decay. These findings exclude $95\%$ confidence level limits on the $\rho$ mass for $m_\rho < 1.5$ TeV, assuming a unit branching fraction. Furthermore, the results constrain the scale of new physics at approximately $1.5$ TeV for a $\rho$ mass of $1.5$ TeV.

This study examines the pressure-induced evolution of the superconducting transition temperature ($T_{\rm C}$) in Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ using high-resolution $^{31}$P NMR. The results indicate that $T_{\rm C}$ increases with pressure, reaching a maximum of 1.75 K at 1.2 GPa, before declining at higher pressures. This behavior is attributed to the pressure-dependent variations in the superconducting gap and the spin-fluctuation-mediated superconducting mechanism.

We demonstrate that an infalling observer experiences a black hole horizon as a "fuzzball," where the duration of their existence before being radiated away is directly proportional to their remaining proper time. This finding supports the fuzzball proposal as a viable resolution to the black hole information paradox.

Neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) serve as a potent tool for modeling vector fields derived from noisy measurements, a technique applicable across diverse fields such as fluid dynamics, neuroscience, and finance. Nevertheless, these models are susceptible to overfitting, which can result in erratic and unpredictable behaviors. This paper introduces a novel regularization strategy designed to constrain the vector field's dynamics, ensuring they remain consistent with prior knowledge. We demonstrate that this approach can be effectively implemented using a neural ODE equipped with a layer-wise adaptive learning rate. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence and illustrate its efficacy through numerical experiments on both synthetic data and real-world applications.

This study introduces a new approach for navigating 3D indoor environments using only a sequence of 2D images. We propose the Object Memory Transformer (OMT), which leverages object-centric memory to facilitate navigation. The OMT framework integrates a transformer-based encoder with a memory module that stores object features. This design allows the system to focus on salient objects, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the input image sequence. We demonstrate that the OMT framework, when combined with a standard transformer-based decoder, achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while utilizing significantly less memory.

This study introduces a novel framework for instruction-tuning that balances performance trade-offs by integrating both the quality and quantity of training data. We propose a two-stage approach: first, we develop a data selection method to identify high-quality samples, followed by a two-stage training process that leverages these samples alongside a broader dataset. Experiments on the DeBERTa-based model using the FEVER dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses the performance of the standard training approach.

This study examines the relationship between participation and learning objectives within the context of informal online communities. Drawing on Lave and Wenger's (1991) theory of legitimate peripheral participation (LPP), we posit that peripheral involvement serves as a foundational step toward engaging in core community activities. We further suggest that this participation style facilitates learning goals, specifically through the acquisition of knowledge and the development of social capital. To test these hypotheses, we analyzed data from a large-scale online forum dedicated to the study of religion. Our findings indicate that LPP is indeed a vital component of learning within such forums, yet they also reveal that peripheral participants often fail to achieve their intended learning goals.

This study introduces a local pseudopotential adaptation of the transcorrelated (TC) method, a many-body wavefunction approach capable of capturing strong electron correlations. The method is applied to metallic systems, specifically the alkali metals Li, Na, and K, as well as solid argon. The results demonstrate that the local pseudopotential TC method achieves accuracy comparable to the random phase approximation (RPA) in describing metallic systems. Furthermore, the method is validated against experimental data for the alkali metals, showing excellent agreement with measured lattice constants, cohesive energies, and bulk moduli.

This study examines the impact of location uncertainty on the Boltzmann equation, utilizing a perturbation approach to derive a new kinetic Fokker-Planck equation. This derived equation incorporates an added damping term, which ensures that the system conserves mass, momentum, and energy indefinitely. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system converges exponentially toward its global Maxwellian equilibrium as time progresses.

The widespread adoption of big data has driven the development of numerous techniques for data storage and processing, with randomization playing a pivotal role in both. In storage, it enhances privacy and data integrity, while in computation, it facilitates secure multi-party computation and differential privacy. This paper introduces a new approach to randomizing data during the MapReduce computation phase, specifically designed to protect sensitive information. The proposed method is highly efficient, requiring only a single bit of randomness per data element, and it operates without altering the original data or its associated keys.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in robotics, enabling robots to master complex tasks through trial-and-error. However, RL agents typically require extensive real-world interaction, which is often impractical due to the risks of hardware damage and the need for expensive equipment. To address this, we introduce SafeAPT, a novel algorithm that adapts policies learned in simulation to real-world robotic settings. SafePT operates by continuously monitoring the discrepancy between predicted and actual state transitions; when a significant deviation occurs, the system halts the current policy and reverts to a safety baseline. This mechanism allows SafePT to achieve rapid adaptation to real-world conditions while ensuring safety. Empirical results demonstrate that SafePT successfully mitigates the sim-to-real gap, enabling robots to learn challenging skills in simulated environments and execute them safely and effectively in the real world.

The Fanaroff-Riley (FR) classification system divides radio galaxies into two distinct categories, FR I and FR II, based on their radio structures and jet characteristics. This study examines the FR classification of radio galaxies within the $z=0.01-0.1$ range, utilizing a sample of 100 objects selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS). We analyze the radio luminosity, jet morphology, and the relationship between radio and optical properties for these sources. Our findings indicate that the FR classification is not a function of redshift, suggesting that the evolution of radio galaxies at low redshifts is not driven by a redshift-dependent mechanism. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between the radio power of FR I and FR II galaxies and the optical power of their host galaxies, a trend that remains consistent across the redshift range examined.

This study introduces a nonparametric testing framework for assessing the significance of regression functions. Unlike existing literature, our approach does not rely on structural assumptions about the functions, such as linearity or monotonicity. Instead, we utilize a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) to define the parameter space and construct a test statistic based on the distance between the observed regression function and a null hypothesis set. Leveraging the Representer Theorem, we derive an explicit formula for this statistic. To address computational challenges associated with high-dimensional kernels, we implement a random projection technique that approximates the statistic with a guaranteed error bound. Finally, we demonstrate the test's asymptotic size control and evaluate its finite-sample performance through simulations and a real-world case study.

This study investigates the efficacy of multilingual versus monolingual models for analyzing social media content. We evaluate these approaches across various tasks, including hate speech detection, language identification, and the classification of hate speech subtypes. Our findings indicate that multilingual models perform comparably to their specialized unilingual counterparts. Furthermore, we examine the impact of data augmentation on performance and identify that these models are particularly vulnerable to errors when processing non-English languages.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is increasingly utilized to diagnose brain disorders, yet the high dimensionality of fMRI data presents significant challenges for classification. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to extract features from fMRI data, achieving superior classification accuracy for brain diseases. The proposed architecture comprises two main components: a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) that processes raw fMRI data to generate a feature vector, and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that utilizes this vector to classify brain states. Experimental results indicate that the 3D CNN effectively captures the spatial relationships between brain regions, thereby enhancing classification performance. Furthermore, the system's efficacy was validated across three distinct brain disorder datasets.

This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing convergence rates in linear systems under dissipative control. By integrating concepts from both control theory and probability theory, the authors establish a fresh framework for rate analysis that leverages the energy dissipation of the closed-loop system to derive bounds on the convergence rate. This approach is particularly advantageous for systems exhibiting complex dynamics, such as those with multiple unstable modes. The proposed method is validated through numerical experiments on a quadrotor system, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving rapid convergence.

This study introduces a boundary treatment approach for high-order numerical schemes that leverages the concept of a non-reflecting boundary condition. By utilizing the characteristic decomposition of the governing equations, the method calculates boundary fluxes through a least-squares minimization process. This technique is designed to enhance both the stability and accuracy of numerical solutions at boundaries. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to various high-order schemes, including finite difference, finite volume, and discontinuous Galerkin methods. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through several test cases, such as the linear wave equation, Burgers' equation, and the Euler equations, with results showing superior performance compared to traditional boundary treatments.

This study investigates the optical absorption of silicon films deposited on photonic crystal back reflectors (PCBRs) featuring silicon nanodisk arrays. By employing a photonic band diagram analysis, we demonstrate that the absorption characteristics of these films are tunable based on film thickness. Specifically, silicon films ranging from 100 nm to 300 nm exhibit enhanced absorption within the 1.1–1.6 μm wavelength range when paired with the PCBR. Furthermore, we analyze the physical mechanisms driving this absorption increase and evaluate the potential for creating ultra-thin, high-efficiency solar cells using this approach.

Valuation algebra serves as a potent framework for managing uncertainty within constraint satisfaction problems. This framework is founded on valuations, which are functions assigning values to variables, and employs local operations to combine and manipulate these valuations. Valuation algebra extends this by utilizing credal sets, which are collections of valuations, and defines fundamental operations such as restriction, marginalization, and combination specifically for these sets. This paper examines the properties of these operations, demonstrating that they adhere to the fundamental duality laws of valuations. We further establish that the duality laws hold for the credal set operations when credal sets are restricted to those that are closed under minimization. Finally, we outline a specific class of credal sets that satisfy these duality laws, even without requiring closure under minimization.

This study introduces a distance-based recommendation model that leverages the Wasserstein distance to measure the similarity between a user and items. The proposed Wasserstein distance is derived from the Kullback-Leibler divergence applied to the cumulative distribution functions of the users' and items' locations. The model's performance is evaluated using the widely used MovieLens-1M dataset, with results compared against various baseline models. The findings indicate that the Wasserstein distance-based approach yields superior recommendation accuracy compared to the baselines.

The paper introduces a new class of non-Markovian channels, termed the "quasi-ENM GAD channel," which exhibits non-Markovian characteristics that differ fundamentally from the standard eternally non-Markovian (ENM) property. Unlike traditional ENM channels, the non-Markovian behavior in the quasi-ENM GAD channel manifests only during specific time intervals, after which the dynamics revert to a Markovian form. This unique dynamic arises from the interaction between memory effects and the specific structure of the environment's spectral density. The study explores the implications of this new class of channels for quantum information processing, highlighting how these quasi-ENM GAD channels can be utilized to enhance the robustness of quantum information against decoherence. The results suggest that by carefully engineering the environment, one can achieve a controlled balance between non-Markovian and Markovian regimes, thereby optimizing the performance of quantum information protocols. The paper also discusses the potential applications of these channels in various quantum technologies, including quantum computing and quantum communication, where the preservation of quantum coherence is crucial. The findings open up new avenues for research in the field of non-Markovian quantum dynamics and its practical applications. The paper concludes by outlining future directions for research in this area, emphasizing the importance of further investigating the properties of quasi-ENM GAD channels and their potential to revolutionize quantum information processing. The study also highlights the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration in advancing the field

This paper introduces CCRAL, a novel approach designed to enhance model generalization for unseen testing data by leveraging the distributional characteristics of training data. Specifically, CCRAL employs a clustering strategy to segment training data into distinct subgroups, each with unique data distributions. Subsequently, it trains specialized models for every cluster, which are then integrated via a weighted voting mechanism to generate the final prediction. This ensemble leverages the diversity of clusters to improve performance on out-of-domain data. We validate CCRAL's effectiveness across various tasks, including image classification, natural language understanding, and text generation, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Creating semantic maps is a critical yet difficult task in robotics, primarily because it requires aligning the semantic labels of an existing geometric map with a scene's semantic segmentation. This paper introduces a new approach that leverages a geometric map to automatically and efficiently generate a semantic hierarchy. By utilizing a graph-based optimization framework, the method aligns the geometric map with a semantic segmentation derived from a reference image, thereby producing a semantic map. This framework is designed to be flexible, supporting various types of geometric maps and segmentation data. Additionally, it incorporates a novel cost function that ensures the resulting semantic map remains consistent with the original segmentation. The paper also details a post-processing stage to convert the hierarchical output into a flat structure. Experimental results demonstrate that the method is effective and efficient, capable of generating semantic maps from RGB-D data in under 10 seconds.

This paper examines the Rikudo puzzle, a logic-based grid challenge where players must determine the count of paths of specific lengths originating from each cell. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for instances where all numbers are odd, and establish NP-completeness for cases containing at least one even number.

This study introduces a novel approach to solving the optimal transport problem by leveraging the Sinkhorn's algorithm. We demonstrate that this method can be reformulated as a specific type of neural network, where the weight matrices are derived from the cost function. This perspective allows us to apply established techniques for training neural networks to optimize the corresponding optimal transport task. Furthermore, we present a new architecture that integrates the Sinkhorn's algorithm with the ResNet model to perform image style transfer. Experimental results indicate that this proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions in style transfer performance.

We report the detection of a quasar at $z=1.81$ in the lens system J0818-2613, alongside a companion deflector at $z=1.41$, utilizing the VLT's Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE). This system, previously identified as a potential lens candidate by the Dark Energy Survey (DES), was also observed by the Keck telescope. Our findings confirm that J0818-2613 is indeed a gravitational lens, with the quasar's light split into two distinct images. We also present a new spectrum for the companion deflector J1817+2729, which contains a broad emission line at $z=1.41$. This spectral data, combined with the redshifts of the two quasars, allows us to calculate the lens system's Hubble constant, $H_0$, yielding $69.0^{+1.8}_{-1.7}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ for J0818-2613 and $69.0^{+1.8}_{-1.7}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ for J1817+2729. This study addresses a generalized $q$-difference equation involving Caputo-type $q$-derivatives. By employing the difference method, the authors formulate an associated initial value problem for a generalized $q$-difference equation featuring a q-summation operator. The work further establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the primary problem utilizing the method of successive approximations.

This study investigates the phonon Hall conductivity in dielectric materials, revealing that it is significantly enhanced by applying a magnetic field. We demonstrate that this phenomenon arises from phonon-phonon scattering, which is driven by the magnetic field-induced modulation of phonon group velocities. Furthermore, we establish that the phonon Hall conductivity is tunable via the magnetic field, with its magnitude governed by parameters such as field strength, temperature, and phonon wavelength.

Wide-field imaging systems are increasingly vital for applications like space weather monitoring and solar physics. However, these setups often suffer from vignetting and reduced sensitivity at field edges, which can be mitigated by using a nod-and-shuffle technique to enhance the field of view. This method involves shifting the detector to capture overlapping images, which are then combined to create a single, wide-field mosaic. This approach significantly cuts down acquisition time, a critical factor given the rapid evolution of solar phenomena. This study evaluates the nod-and-shuffle technique using a custom-built, wide-field, high-resolution spectropolarimeter designed for the solar photosphere. We present the instrument's design, its performance characteristics, and the resulting data. This study establishes novel matrix extensions of the Gr\"uss-type inequalities previously derived by the author in reference [10]. Specifically, it derives fresh matrix inequalities that generalize the previously established Gruss-type inequalities.

This study examines the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) within the context of spherically symmetric black hole formation and evaporation. We demonstrate that the ANEC is violated during the black hole's evaporation phase. Furthermore, we establish that the ANEC is not satisfied even in the stationary state of a black hole.

This study examines the trace anomaly in a four-dimensional Conformal Field Theory (CFT) featuring an irrelevant operator with a conformal dimension $\Delta$ that is an integer. We demonstrate that such a model allows for a continuous variation of the anomaly coefficients $a$ and $c$ between those of a free scalar field and those of a free fermion. Furthermore, we establish that the ratio $a/c$ spans the entire interval $[1/2, 2]$.

This study introduces a maturity model for ICS testbeds, designed to evaluate their current capabilities and guide future enhancements. Drawing from the essential characteristics of ICS testbeds and the specific needs of their users, the research proposes a four-level maturity framework. To operationalize this model, a set of assessment criteria is established, each with a defined scoring range. The model's validity is confirmed through a case study involving an ICS testbed developed by the University of Tehran.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has recently gained significant attention, yet the complexity of learning in multi-agent environments remains a major obstacle. This paper introduces a novel greedy-based value representation (GVR) designed to enhance multi-agent learning performance. The GVR framework employs a greedy strategy to select a subset of agents for estimating the value of the entire group, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the value function. This approach enables the model to capture the impact of individual agents on global outcomes while maintaining high performance. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that GVR can achieve an optimal value function under specific conditions. Empirical evaluations across various MARL scenarios confirm that the GVR method outperforms existing techniques.

Stereotypical biases in language models pose a significant risk to their deployment in real-world applications. To address this, we introduce StereoSet, a dataset designed to evaluate such biases across four domains: gender, race, age, and occupation. Unlike previous efforts, StereoSet offers a comprehensive, large-scale resource that includes 100,000 sentence pairs, covering these diverse domains. We have developed a novel metric, "StereoEval," to assess the degree of bias in these models. Our analysis reveals that while current language models exhibit minimal gender bias, they suffer from significant bias across the other domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fine-tuning on the StereoSet dataset effectively mitigates these stereotypical patterns.

This study introduces a novel, data-driven approach for optimizing network tilt settings, which are crucial for managing cell interference and coverage. The problem is modeled as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework, where each "arm" represents a specific tilt configuration. The Contextual Multi-Armed-Bandit (CMAB) framework is employed to develop a learning algorithm capable of acquiring tilt update policies. The proposed method, named "Tilt-RL," utilizes a deep neural network to learn these policies, with the network's parameters refined through an online learning process. The paper also presents a theoretical analysis of the Tilt-RL algorithm, demonstrating that it converges to an optimal policy. Furthermore, the study includes numerical experiments that validate the effectiveness of this approach.

This study aims to extend complex symmetry in convex geometry by linking it to convex body characterization through sections and projections. We demonstrate that a convex domain is a complex symmetric body precisely when all its one-dimensional slices exhibit complex symmetry. We also provide a corresponding complex symmetric criterion regarding projections in the case of circular bodies. These findings are applied to show that Hilbert spaces remain complex symmetric under small perturbations.

The rise of the digital economy has sparked significant debate regarding the marketization of personal data. While scholars have extensively analyzed this phenomenon, they have largely overlooked the role of laypeople in shaping it. This paper presents a study on how ordinary individuals assess transactions involving their personal data. We conducted a survey with 1,000 participants, asking them to evaluate 100 hypothetical data transactions across various dimensions. Our findings reveal that lay evaluations often contradict current market frameworks; this divergence stems from a lack of clarity about the nature of personal data transactions and the specific roles data plays within them. Furthermore, we identified that certain data types are more likely to be viewed as marketable, and that specific transaction characteristics significantly influence the perceived marketability of a transaction.

This study introduces a deep learning approach for detecting Frequency-Offseted Time-Neyman (FTN) signaling. By leveraging deep neural networks, the method achieves a substantial reduction in detection complexity, enabling the identification of the transmitted symbol sequence. The architecture utilizes a multi-layered structure to perform sequential detection of symbols. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed scheme offers a significant advantage over traditional FTN detection techniques. Furthermore, the paper evaluates the method's performance through simulations, confirming that it achieves near-ideal results.

This paper investigates the topological characteristics of effect algebras, specifically examining their order topology and Frink ideal topology. We establish that in a complete atomic distributive lattice, these two topologies coincide if and only if the lattice possesses an integer unit. Furthermore, we define a special class of distributive lattices characterized by having an integer unit, noting that this property is equivalent to the lattice being isomorphic to a sublattice of a complete Boolean algebra.

Data augmentation is a critical component of deep learning, particularly for object detection, where it is essential for achieving robust performance. While numerous augmentation techniques have been developed, they often fail to address the specific challenges inherent to detection tasks. This paper introduces SaliencyMix, a novel augmentation strategy that leverages the saliency maps of a trained model to enhance its performance. The approach operates in two stages: initially, a base model is trained using standard techniques; subsequently, this model is fine-tuned with SaliencyMix, which generates augmented images by blending a source image with a target image selected based on its saliency map. The resulting images are created by interpolating the source and target images according to their saliency values. Experimental results on the MS COCO 2017 detection task demonstrate that SaliencyMix achieves a 2.0% improvement in AP over the baseline, surpassing other state-of-the-art methods. The project's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhaozhiyuan/SaliencyMix.

In 1988, Vershik and Kerov provided a full classification of indecomposable positive traces on the Iwahori--Hecke algebra $\Heck_q(\tilde{A}_1)$ for $q \in (0,1)$, a result that had remained unresolved for Iwahori--Hecke algebras of types $B$, $C$, and $D$ until now. This paper rectifies that omission by presenting a complete set of indecomposable positive traces on these specific algebras.

This study examines the alignment of galaxy shapes, a phenomenon that can signal violations of statistical isotropy in the universe. We introduce a novel statistical framework designed to detect such alignments, which are also relevant to the study of intrinsic shape correlations within modified gravity. Our approach utilizes an alignment parameter that quantifies the deviation from isotropy, serving as a sensitive indicator of anisotropic large-scale structures. Furthermore, we show that the parameter can be expressed as a linear combination of the galaxy two-point correlation function's multipole moments. Soft-deformable particle systems, such as those composed of self-propelled active rods, exhibit complex dynamics that diverge significantly from passive counterparts. This study investigates the viscoelastic response of such systems, specifically focusing on their memory properties. We analyze a system of active rods confined within a 2D harmonic potential, subjected to a stepwise strain applied to the confinement. Upon reversing the strain, the system displays a delayed relaxation, indicating the presence of memory. This phenomenon is driven by the persistent internal stresses generated during the deformation phase, which persist within the system's structure. Furthermore, the relaxation kinetics are governed by the interplay between passive viscoelasticity and active self-propulsion forces, resulting in a non-exponential decay profile that varies with the duration of the prior deformation. These findings underscore the critical role of active mechanisms in shaping the dynamic behavior of soft matter systems, offering new insights into the design of adaptive materials capable of storing and releasing mechanical energy.

This study examines the phase transitions of gold nanoparticles (NPs) using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We analyzed the thermodynamic stability of NPs with varying sizes, ranging from 1.2 nm to 3.5 nm, by calculating the Gibbs free energy of the liquid and solid phases. Our findings indicate that smaller gold NPs exhibit a higher melting temperature compared to larger ones. Furthermore, we investigated the melting process by examining the Gibbs free energy difference between the liquid and solid phases. We also evaluated the entropy and enthalpy changes associated with phase transitions to determine the driving forces behind melting. Our results demonstrate that the Gibbs free energy difference serves as an effective metric for assessing the thermodynamic stability of gold nanoparticles.

This study examines the impact of relaxing standard differentiability requirements on the analysis of quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problems, specifically within the context of the Keller-Segel system. We demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, these relaxed differentiability assumptions do not alter the existence or multiplicity of solutions. This conclusion is achieved by employing test function methods and applying a fundamental identity for Sobolev norms.

This study introduces a minimal extension of the Standard Model featuring a $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ gauge symmetry, which incorporates a gauge boson and a right-handed neutrino. The framework is designed to address both observed horizontal anomalies and the origin of neutrino masses. The model generates a correlation between quarks and anti-letons, which explains the observed anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and the discrepancy in the muon-to-electron ratio. Furthermore, it predicts a correlation between the muon $g-2$ anomaly and the magnitude of neutrinoless double-beta decay, which can be tested by future experiments.

This study establishes several identities related to $(h; q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials by employing the $p$-adic $i\ntegral$ on $\Z_p$ as well as the $p$-adic logarithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the validity of these results through numerical verification.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning framework for addressing nonstationary reward estimation problems. We present a novel algorithm that integrates a weighted combination of the UCB1 index with a weighted average estimator. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's regret, establishing an upper bound that relies on the nonstationarity of average rewards. Furthermore, we evaluate the algorithm's performance through simulations and a real-world experiment involving a smart home environment.

This paper introduces a novel causal effect measure, the Causal Odds Ratio (COR), designed to address scenarios where both exposure and outcome are binary. We demonstrate that the COR is mathematically equivalent to the ratio of two causal risk odds, thereby inheriting the interpretability characteristic of traditional odds ratios. Furthermore, we establish the consistency of the COR estimator within large-sample frameworks and prove its robustness against unmeasured confounding through sensitivity analysis. We also derive a closed-form expression for the Causal Prevalence Odds Ratio (CPOP), a related concept, and illustrate its practical utility through an application to a real-world dataset.

Autoencoders are a widely used class of generative models, typically built from stacks of invertible layers. However, the standard training procedure for these models often fails to adequately optimize the variational lower bound on log-likelihood. This paper introduces a novel training strategy that directly maximizes the log-likelihood, demonstrating that it yields superior results in both sample quality and likelihood scores compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm for computing the gradient of the variational likelihood estimator, which is applicable to both discrete and continuous data types.

Smart cities are rapidly expanding, generating vast amounts of data that are often difficult to analyze and visualize. This study introduces a visualization platform designed to help users comprehend complex data through interactive, dynamic, and intuitive graphical representations. The system's core is a data processing engine that employs a machine learning pipeline to automatically extract meaningful insights from raw inputs. To achieve this, we have developed a new framework for unsupervised anomaly detection that integrates both unsupervised learning and data mining techniques. This framework utilizes a specialized data mining algorithm to identify anomalous data points, which are then converted into visual representations to aid in the interpretation of smart city datasets.

This study introduces optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners tailored for Hybridizable Discontinuous Galerkin (HdGc) linear systems. By employing a straightforward grid refinement strategy and a novel coarse space construction, we achieve a spectrum of multigrid iteration operators that remains bounded and independent of polynomial degree. Consequently, the resulting preconditioned multigrid method delivers convergence rates that are both optimal and geometry-independent. We further demonstrate that these preconditioned schemes are inherently parallelizable, with their convergence performance remaining robust regardless of the number of processors used. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate these findings.

The E-value serves as a metric for assessing robustness against unmeasured confounding. This study extends the concept to scenarios involving missing data, deriving a novel formula for the missing-data E-value that incorporates observed data, missingness mechanisms, and the probability of missingness conditional on treatment and outcome. We demonstrate that the conditional probability can be estimated using a sensitivity model, enabling the calculation of the missing-data E-value through a two-stage sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, we prove that the resulting missing-data E-value is lower than or equal to the observed-data counterpart, indicating that missing data can diminish the robustness of causal inferences. We illustrate these methods with a simulation study and a real-world application involving the link between statin use and dementia risk.

In crossover trials, particularly those involving few participants, missing data poses a significant challenge. This study examines the impact of missing data on the evaluation of treatment effects in such contexts, specifically focusing on the analysis of treatment differences. We introduce a novel approach to estimate these differences that explicitly accounts for the missing data mechanism. This method is grounded in a Bayesian framework utilizing a mixture model to handle the missingness. We demonstrate the approach's performance through a simulation analysis and apply it to a clinical trial assessing the efficacy of a new treatment versus standard care for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

This study introduces a novel DRAM Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) that leverages the inherent variations in DRAM memory cells. The proposed architecture is designed to be highly secure, robust, and straightforward to implement. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art DRAM PUFs regarding both robustness and throughput. Furthermore, the system can be extended to generate keys for other types of memory, such as MRAM and PRAM, by utilizing their respective read and write operations.

Virtualization has fundamentally transformed network management, enabling the rapid orchestration of network functions and services. However, the intricate nature of these virtualized environments has made orchestration increasingly complex, a challenge that has been mitigated by the adoption of open-source, cloud-native platforms like Kubernetes. This paper examines the application of functional programming within the Go language to build such orchestration systems. We argue that Go's functional programming capabilities are particularly well-suited for this domain, as they facilitate the creation of modular, reusable, and composable components. These elements are essential for managing the dynamic and sophisticated requirements of virtualized networks.

The toric code serves as a vital benchmark for evaluating quantum gate performance, yet its extensive gate count renders it impractical for current hardware. To address this, we introduce a streamlined, linear-time algorithm for calculating the ground state of the toric code on a square lattice. This approach effectively bypasses the limitations of the traditional Bravyi-Gosset algorithm, which incurs a quadratic gate overhead.

The Universal Worker System (UWS) is a distributed framework designed to facilitate job execution within large-scale computing clusters. It enables a flexible, multi-tenancy environment where numerous users can concurrently submit jobs to the system. UWS operates by distributing workers across the cluster, allowing each to execute tasks assigned by a central coordinator. This coordinator manages the allocation of jobs to workers and oversees the cluster's resource scheduling. To ensure efficient resource utilization, the system employs a sophisticated task allocation strategy that incorporates both the specific requirements of each task and the available resources of each worker.

This study introduces a novel framework for integrating blockchain with wireless communications and networking systems, aiming to enhance the capabilities of these domains. Blockchain serves as a distributed ledger that records all transactions within a network, thereby enabling the development of transparent, secure, and efficient wireless systems. We present a comprehensive overview of the key components of blockchain-enabled wireless systems, including their underlying principles, operational mechanisms, and specific applications. Furthermore, we examine the primary challenges associated with this field, such as scalability, privacy, and security, while also exploring future research directions. The paper concludes by highlighting several promising avenues for further investigation, including the use of blockchain for distributed resource allocation, authentication, and the protection of user privacy.

The detection of oxygen (O2) and ozone (O3) in terrestrial exoplanet atmospheres is often proposed as a biosignature for life. However, these species can also accumulate in the abiotic atmospheres of planets with high CO2 levels, particularly in the habitable zone. This study investigates how the host star's temperature influences the relationship between O2 and O3 in such planets. We utilized a 1D radiative-convective model to simulate atmospheres of Earth-like and Venus-like planets orbiting stars with effective temperatures ranging from 3,000 to 6,000 K. Our findings indicate that the correlation between O2 and O3 is not universal; it varies based on the host star's temperature and the planet's atmospheric composition. Furthermore, we observed that O3 concentrations can reach levels comparable to Earth's, even in the absence of biological activity. Consequently, the presence of O2 and O3 alone cannot definitively confirm the existence of life on these planets.

We demonstrate that surface currents within both bosonic and fermionic topological systems exhibit robustness against disorder and open boundary conditions. This phenomenon arises from the non-Hermitian Poincar\'e monodromy theorem, which establishes a link between surface currents and the non-Hermitian spectral flow. We further show that this effect persists even in the presence of disorder, provided the system remains non-Hermitian. This finding is supported by numerical simulations of disordered bosonic and fermionic lattice models. Our results suggest that surface currents are a universal property of non-Hermitian topological systems, offering a promising avenue for future experimental verification.

This study introduces a domain-adapted multilingual neural machine translation (MNT) model designed for medical applications. The approach involves fine-tuning a pre-trained MNT model on a specific dataset of English-to-German medical sentence pairs. The resulting system is evaluated against an out-of-domain baseline using a held-out test set, with a detailed analysis of the performance gap between in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios. The findings demonstrate that the fine-tuned model significantly outperforms the general translation model within the medical domain.

This study examines the formation of solitary and shock structures within a magnetized, collisional, and dusty plasma environment featuring negative ions and a non-Maxwellian electron distribution. Utilizing the reductive perturbation technique, we derive the non-linear ion-acoustic (LIA) equation and analyze how these structures emerge. The analysis reveals that the ion fluid temperature and the non-thermal electron parameter are pivotal in determining the characteristics of both solitary and shock waves. Specifically, the non-linear coefficient is found to be positive, indicating that only compressive non-linear waves can form. Furthermore, we observe that the non-thermal electron parameter significantly influences the width of solitons and the amplitude of both solitons and shocks. The findings are illustrated through numerical simulations, and the results are discussed in relation to space plasma environments.

This paper introduces a new multilingual sentence representation learning approach that utilizes the contrastive context prediction (CCP) task. The objective of CCP is to forecast the context surrounding a sentence based on its content. Theoretically, this framework encourages the model to acquire representations that are both semantically meaningful and contextually informative. To achieve this, we develop a multilingual masked language model (MLM) that jointly trains on two tasks: the CCP task and a multilingual masked language modeling (MLM) task. The latter involves predicting masked tokens within a sentence. The proposed method is evaluated on the sentence retrieval task, where it demonstrates superior performance over existing state-of-the-art baselines.

This paper introduces a novel multimodal learning approach called Prototypical Modality Rebalance (PMR), designed to mitigate the performance gap between fast and slow modalities. Unlike prior methods that rely on external mechanisms to equalize learning speeds, PMR focuses on enhancing the learning efficiency of slower modalities through the use of prototypical networks. By establishing class-specific prototypes for each modality, PMR enables the extraction of discriminative features that are both modality- and class-aware. These refined features facilitate the learning of more robust and discriminative representations for slower modalities, thereby reducing the disparity in learning speed. Experimental results across various benchmarks demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the performance of slow modalities and substantially boosts overall multimodal performance.

We examine the kinetic equations governing massless fermions in a conformally invariant background, specifically within the framework of the eikonal approximation. Our findings reveal that the divergence of the local particle number density is intrinsically tied to the divergence of the local energy density. This relationship enables the formulation of a transport equation for the particle number density that incorporates a novel dissipative term, which we analyze to determine its impact on particle number evolution.

This study introduces a novel command recognition framework that integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to enhance the efficiency of acoustic feature processing. The proposed architecture, designated as CNN+(TT-DNN), leverages the CNN to extract and compress spatial information from the input, thereby reducing the data volume required by the subsequent DNN. Experimental evaluations were conducted using the CMU-ARCTIC command corpus, which features 100 distinct commands and a dataset of 1,000 utterances per command. The results demonstrate that the CNN+(TT-DNN) model achieves a 10% improvement in command recognition accuracy compared to a traditional CNN, while simultaneously utilizing 100 times fewer parameters.

This study examines the deterministic evolution of a quantum system governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, driven by a system-bath interaction that is controllable via external inputs. We demonstrate that the non-Hermitian dynamics can be faithfully replicated by an equivalent Hermitian system, wherein the latter's Hamiltonian explicitly depends on the external driving forces. By establishing this correspondence, we establish a framework for manipulating quantum processes described by non-Hermitian operators through external control.

We introduce a novel plasmonic solar cell design that utilizes a single aluminum nanoparticle to boost photocurrent in thin-film silicon cells. This approach offers a straightforward, low-cost pathway to achieve high conversion efficiencies. The device employs a single aluminum nanoparticle positioned on a dielectric layer above the silicon cell, which is further backed by a reflective metal layer. The photocurrent generated by the plasmonic structure is calculated using the optical scattering cross-section of the particle. We demonstrate that this method can enhance photocurrent by up to 100% and achieve a maximum conversion efficiency of 14.2% with an optimal particle radius of 30 nm.

This study introduces an algebra of binary relations that integrates linear-time modal dynamic logic, specifically designed to model the computational steps of a transition system. By utilizing this algebraic framework, we can establish a formal treatment of the halting problem and demonstrate that it is undecidable. Furthermore, we prove that the algebra itself is undecidable, thereby indicating that a uniform solution for model checking within this context does not exist.

This study introduces a novel, end-to-end tensor-based hardware architecture for deep neural networks, termed FDHT-LSTM. By integrating Fast Discrete Hartley Transforms (FDHT) with Low-Rank Tensor Decomposition, the FDHT-LSTM framework delivers superior performance in both accuracy and efficiency compared to existing tensor-decomposition-based hardware solutions. The architecture is evaluated using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, demonstrating a throughput increase of 1.6x to 2.0x and an energy efficiency gain of 1.4x to 1.8x over current state-of-the-art hardware. Furthermore, the FDHT-LSTM framework is benchmarked against the TensorFlow-Lite (TFLite) software implementation, achieving a 1.4x to 1.6x improvement in energy efficiency and a 1.2x to 1.4x improvement in throughput.

UAVs are increasingly utilized in diverse sectors, including military, commercial, and civil aviation. While MAVLink serves as a prevalent communication protocol for UAVs, its lack of inherent security necessitates the implementation of encryption to safeguard message integrity and confidentiality. This study evaluates various encryption algorithms to determine the most effective solution for securing UAVs using the MAVLink protocol. The research assesses the performance of five algorithms—AES, ChaCha20, RC4, Twofish, and Blowfish—by measuring their computational efficiency and analyzing their resistance to common attacks. The findings indicate that ChaCha20 is the optimal choice, offering the highest efficiency alongside robust protection against known cryptographic threats.

This paper introduces a methodology for deriving network emulation models that are tailored to specific application requirements. By leveraging the emergence of end-to-end characteristics, the proposed approach significantly simplifies the emulation of the underlying network infrastructure. This simplification enables the emulation of a broader spectrum of real-world networks, including those with varying levels of reliability and security. Furthermore, the method facilitates the creation of emulation models that are both more computationally efficient and easier to configure.

We present a novel, geometrically invariant formulation of the Newman-Penrose map, which establishes a correspondence between the conformal compactification of Minkowski space and the complex projective null flag manifold. By re-expressing the Newman-Penrose map twistorially, we derive a representation that maintains invariance under geometric transformations, surpassing the coordinate-dependent nature of the original construction. This study also investigates the infinitesimal variations of the map and their realization as vector fields on the null flag manifold. Furthermore, we explore the correspondence between these vector fields and elements of the conformal algebra, demonstrating that the differential of the Newman-Penrose map induces a homomorphism from the conformal algebra to the Lie algebra of vector fields on the null flag manifold.

Cosmic ray muon telescopes are increasingly utilized in archaeology for non-invasive scanning of ancient structures and in medical imaging to visualize human anatomy. This paper introduces a novel design for such telescopes, featuring a 3D printed plastic scintillator tracker that enables the reconstruction of muon trajectories. The system's performance was validated using simulated data, with the results demonstrating that the device can effectively reconstruct muon paths with a momentum exceeding 3 GeV/c.

This work introduces PEGLL, a new parsing algorithm that extends the capabilities of the existing EGG algorithm. While the EGG algorithm is an extension of the PEG algorithm designed to support left recursion, the newly proposed PEGLL algorithm further enhances this by accommodating additional forms of mutual left recursion. This advancement allows the algorithm to handle a broader range of recursive grammars compared to the EGG algorithm.

This study examines the spontaneous radiative decay of a scalar particle into a fermion-antifermion pair, a process that is kinematically permitted only when the scalar's mass exceeds twice the fermion mass. The analysis focuses on the radiation spectrum emitted by a uniformly accelerated scalar particle within the context of Unruh-DeWitt detectors. The study derives the radiation rate as a function of the scalar's mass, the fermion mass, and the detector's acceleration. The findings indicate that at infinite temperature, the radiation rate vanishes despite the process remaining kinematically allowed, a result attributed to the thermal suppression of the fermionic vacuum state.

This study investigates how linguistic context influences the prediction of word predictability and its correlation with surprise annotations. We introduce a new dataset featuring 1,000 sentences, each containing a target word, paired with corresponding human ratings of surprise. To evaluate the predictive power of various linguistic contexts, we compare traditional co-occurrence statistics against modern contextualized embeddings. Our findings indicate that longer linguistic contexts substantially enhance predictions of surprise ratings, with contextualized embeddings outperforming static co-occurrence measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the semantic nuances captured by contextualized embeddings are critical for accurately modeling the relationship between word predictability and the resulting element of surprise.

This study introduces a new approach to 3D object estimation that learns canonical poses from single-view images. We developed a multi-stage training scheme that progressively refines pose estimation accuracy, enabling the model to master subtle pose variations. Additionally, we designed a new loss function to enhance the robustness of the pose estimation. Our method was evaluated on the 3DObjectDetectNet benchmark, where it achieved state-of-the-art results.

We investigate the spin-orbit coupling in InSb nanowires, which enables the manipulation of inter-quantum-dot coupling through external magnetic fields. This interaction facilitates the creation of spin-dependent, tunable double quantum dots (DQBs) that function as qubits. Our analysis of the resulting two-particle system reveals that the spin-orbit coupling significantly influences the energy spectrum and charge stability diagram. We demonstrate that the spin-orbit interaction can be effectively managed via magnetic field application, allowing for the electrical tuning of inter-dot coupling. Furthermore, we establish that the spin-orbit coupling can be precisely adjusted by modifying the gate voltage.

This study examines the impact of pitch-angle scattering on particle acceleration within 2D simulations of relativistic shocks. By incorporating this effect, we aim to bridge the gap between idealized 1D models and full 3D representations. Our findings indicate that pitch-angle scattering significantly alters particle energy distributions, thereby modifying the inferred properties of the resulting non-thermal population. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these scattered simulations yield shock luminosity values that align with those observed in full 3D models.

The LHC's measurement of the Higgs diphoton decay rate offers a potent means to investigate the Hstrahlung process and extended scalar sectors. This study examines the sensitivity of Hstrahlung to new physics within a model featuring an additional scalar singlet, specifically analyzing how the singlet's mass and mixing angle influence the signal. We demonstrate that, in the limit of a highly massive singlet, the diphoton decay rate converges to the Standard Model prediction. Conversely, in the case of a light singlet, the observed rate can deviate substantially from this expectation.

This study introduces the notion of the joint numerical radius for a collection of operators within a Hilbert space. We examine several of its fundamental properties and demonstrate how the joint numerical radius can be expressed as the solution to specific best approximation problems. Additionally, we explore the connection between the joint operator range and the operators' joint numerical radius.

Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) and Privacy Amplification by Iteration (PAI-IT) are two prominent methods for ensuring privacy in machine learning. While DP-SGD is widely adopted in financial sectors, the PATE framework offers an alternative that is often easier to implement. This study evaluates the performance of both approaches across various financial applications, revealing that they deliver comparable privacy-utility trade-offs. Consequently, the findings suggest that practitioners can confidently select the PATE framework as a viable option.

The established Wold-type decomposition for multivariate second-order random distribution fields is extended to accommodate a broader range of scenarios. This generalized decomposition is subsequently utilized to characterize the general spectral structure of such fields.

This study examines the ignition of a laser in a gas mixture containing dust or other impurities. The ignition process is modeled as a two-stage event: first, the laser irradiation triggers a rapid thermal explosion of the gas, and second, this explosion wave interacts with the dust particles. The analysis focuses on a homogeneous system where dust is evenly dispersed throughout the gas. The research investigates the influence of dust's physical and chemical characteristics on the overall ignition dynamics. The findings indicate that the laser's role is confined to initiating gas ignition; the dust does not alter the fundamental ignition mechanism within the gas itself. However, the dust significantly impacts the post-ignition evolution of the system, notably by modifying the propagation speed of the resulting flame.

This paper introduces a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BASN), designed to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation by explicitly modeling object boundaries. We also present a new dataset, the "Boundary-Aware Segmentation Dataset" (BADS), which includes pixel-level boundary annotations for 10 object classes across 1,000 images. Experimental results demonstrate that BASN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in refining boundary precision. Furthermore, we developed practical applications based on this network, including a real-time segmentation system for autonomous driving and a boundary-aware image editing tool.

This paper introduces the Driver Messenger System (DMS), a framework designed to facilitate safe lane changes by enabling drivers to request assistance from other drivers. The system allows the requesting driver to send a request to a nearby vehicle, which then evaluates the request and responds with either approval or rejection. DMS is designed to complement, not replace, the Lane Change Assistance System (LAS). While LAS relies on vehicle sensors to provide warnings for safe lane changes, it may occasionally fail to detect safe conditions due to limitations in sensor range or accuracy. DMS addresses these limitations by utilizing human drivers as additional sensors; through the exchange of requests and responses, the two vehicles can collectively assess safety more comprehensively. Additionally, DMS aims to enhance driver awareness of upcoming lane changes and foster cooperation among drivers. The study also presents a simulation environment for testing DMS and reports findings from initial experiments.

This study examines the interaction between active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles and various geometrical boundaries, including flat surfaces, spherical shells, and solid spheres. We demonstrate that the behavior of these particles near such interfaces can be analyzed using the image method, which is also applicable to passive Brownian particles. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for the steady-state distribution functions within spherical shells and spheres, as well as the radial flux for particles near flat surfaces.

Siegert states, which represent continuum solutions to the Schrödinger equation, are widely utilized in atomic and molecular electronic structure calculations. This study extends their application to the average atom model, a framework essential for computing atomic properties relevant to dense plasmas. We demonstrate that Siegert states are highly effective for the average atom model, offering a significant reduction in the energy spectrum required to accurately compute atomic properties. This approach is particularly advantageous for neutral and low-ionization states, where the energy levels closely resemble those of isolated atoms. We present calculations of atomic data for carbon, oxygen, and argon, including ionization energies, photoionization cross-sections, and oscillator strengths. Our results align well with existing literature, and we also evaluate the impact of the screening potential on these Siegert states.

This study examines the Si IV 10926 Å line in the 10-minute interval preceding and following a solar flare, utilizing data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS). The analysis reveals a secondary component of the Si IV line with a redshift of approximately 10 km/s, which is notably absent in the line profiles recorded before the flare. This redshifted component is most prominent in the lower atmosphere, specifically within the chromosphere, and is associated with plasma outflows detected by the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA). Furthermore, the intensity of this secondary component correlates with the intensity of the AIA 171 Å emission, suggesting that the redshifted Si IV line serves as a reliable indicator for identifying plasma outflows.

This study examines the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) analysis of the strong CP problem, which posits that the parameter theta is exactly zero. We demonstrate that when theta is non-zero, this framework fails to resolve the issue, evidenced by the fact that the parameter remains free and unconstrained by the theory. Furthermore, we argue that the so-called strong CP problem itself is fundamentally flawed. We contend that the apparent anomaly arises solely from the incorrect assumption that the phase of the quark mass matrix must be real; in reality, the phase can be arbitrary. By allowing this phase to vary, the theory naturally yields an effective theta equal to zero, thereby eliminating the problem entirely.

Consequently, we establish that all $(k,r)$-metric approximate groups within such bounded exponent settings are necessarily approximate groups. This finding resolves an inquiry raised by E. Breuillard, I. Gorodnik, and A. Zucker.

We introduce novel algorithms leveraging Nesterov smoothing and randomization to accelerate the computation of maximum likelihood estimators for log-concave distributions. These methods are designed to be straightforward to implement and execute efficiently, relying on the Frank-Wolfe approach to solve the dual problem of maximum likelihood estimation. Theoretical analysis confirms that both deterministic and randomized variants achieve a convergence rate of $O(1/t)$, with the deterministic version offering an additional guarantee of statistical efficiency. Empirical results indicate that these new methods outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques regarding both speed and accuracy.

The non-interacting rigid arch model serves as a robust framework for examining the statistical mechanics of granular assemblies, offering a novel perspective on the stability of such systems. By analyzing the stability of a single arch, researchers can determine the stability of the entire assembly. This paper introduces a new method for calculating the distribution of stable arches within a two-dimensional granular system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of stable single arches can be derived from the distribution of stable configurations of the whole assembly.

This paper examines a game played on a graph where two players, A and B, alternately select vertices, beginning with A. The primary objective is to maximize (for A) or minimize (for B) the count of distinct vertices visited during the game. The final score is the count of distinct vertices visited in an optimal game starting from a given vertex $v$, and the graph's domination number is defined as the minimum score when the game begins with A at any vertex. The study investigates the domination number for several graph classes, including trees, cycles, paths, wheels, complete bipartite graphs, and graphs with a maximum degree of 4.

The spectral density of stochastic processes is employed to differentiate between random motion types, such as Brownian motion and Levy flights. This study introduces a novel approach to estimating the spectral density of continuous-time stochastic processes by utilizing the autocorrelation function of the corresponding discrete-time process. This technique is particularly advantageous for its straightforward implementation and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to scenarios where the continuous-time process is not directly observable, but rather through indirect measurements.
